body_markdown:
Few things are as exciting as picking up a project car. It’s easy to get carried away with what *could be* and forget to think about what *actually is* . A project car is a problem we knowingly acquire. Whether we intend to solve the problem or learn a little from trying doesn’t particularly matter; project cars care little for what we want. They have their own plans, and the more you’ve played with rotten sheet metal, crusty hardware, or leaking powertrains, the less you’ll be surprised by what your new purchase has in store for you.


Think of it as a hazing ritual carried out by old vehicles; aging vehicles tend to ensure that the owner will encounter a few shared experiences with other car owners. One might own a car for a while without getting mixed up in these, but on a long enough timeline we all get to experience the problems—and joys of solving them—that every good project car carries with it. Here are four examples.


## Paperwork


It’s only a car if you can drive it, and legally driving it is best.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Cars, for better or worse, are items that can often only be enjoyed on the road with paperwork proving you own the thing. While processes exist to replace lost paperwork, or to create fresh documents for a project built from parts, ask anyone who has put themselves through this wringer ,and they will likely tell you to put in the effort to get the paperwork sorted at the time of purchase. You don’t want the hurdles of paying back registration fees, sorting ownership disputes, and heading back and forth repeatedly to to the DMV standing between you and going for a drive. And those items are just the[start of the frustration](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/looking-for-a-winter-project-get-your-paperwork-in-order/) that can come from buying a project without a title or other ownership paperwork. That’s probably why a good project comes with documents.


## A good windshield


Rob Siegel


Think[finding mechanical parts](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/5-levels-of-parts-finding-for-vintage-cars/) is tough? Try to find a windshield for a car that’s been out of production for decades. While 3D printing and other manufacturing techniques have helped reduce the problem of rare parts, glass is one of the areas on a car where sourcing replacements has not gotten easier. Windshields are rarely designed with multiple models in mind, so it’s often not even a cross-reference game for part numbers to get your hands on something clear and ready to install. Either glass exists, and it will be expensive and stressful to ship, or it doesn’t exist, and you are left looking around and through that crack because the project that followed you home didn’t have good glass.


## That intangible thing that makes you love it


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


It’s not something easy to describe, but considering a project car will often test your patience and mental fortitude at some point, it is best to have some kind of connection beyond “it was there, and I could have it.” Even the projects that followed me home on the basis of opportunity have something else that draws me to them. My 1985 Corvette was an impulse purchase with the[idea of an engine swap](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/i-almost-couldnt-cut-the-v-8-heart-out-of-my-corvette/) in mind, but I also love the shape of the rear end of the early fourth-generation Corvette. This ensures that even if the only thing I can do with the car today is stare at it, I’ll at least have positive thoughts while I’m looking at it.


## A bolt that will make you question everything


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


It could be a bolt’s unmovable nature, or the inaccessible placement of a fastener, but the fact is every project will have at least one piece of hardware that will cause a headache. Lots of project cars have been subjected to both the torment of daily use, the horrors of long-term storage, and often a lack of use. Lots of heat cycles can stick nuts and bolts as if they were welded, but rust and corrosion can be worse, literally turning two pieces of metal into one.


New or old, it’s inevitable that there will be a task that will require not only contortions, cursing, the proper tools, and a little bit of luck. More often than not, that will boil down to one piece of hardware. We wish you luck.


Are these the only four features of a good project car? Hardly. If anything, they might be the most common. Surely there are plenty more based on the types of projects you play with and where you are located. Think we missed one? Leave yours in a comment below.
